Ed McMahon, the genial announcer and television personality who spent three decades at Johnny Carson’s side on “The Tonight Show,” died at the age of 86. His career spanned much of the history of American television and included work as a host, pitchman, actor and master of ceremonies, but he remained best known for the booming introduction that became a national catchphrase: “Heeeeere’s Johnny!”

McMahon joined Carson in 1957 as the announcer on the daytime quiz show “Who Do You Trust?” When Carson took over “The Tonight Show” in 1962, McMahon followed him to late-night television. He remained there until Carson retired in 1992, serving as announcer, comic partner and reassuring on-air companion through thousands of broadcasts.

His duties appeared simple: introduce the host, laugh at the jokes, keep the conversation moving and occasionally absorb a well-timed insult. McMahon, however, turned those responsibilities into a distinctive form of performance. His resonant voice, expressive laughter and instinctive timing gave Carson both an audience and a foil. He knew when to encourage a joke, when to react with exaggerated delight and, just as importantly, when to step aside.

The relationship worked because McMahon never seemed to compete with Carson. Instead, he helped create the relaxed atmosphere that made viewers feel they were spending the end of the evening with two familiar friends. Carson frequently teased him about his size, his drinking and his willingness to endorse products, while McMahon responded with good humor and an unmistakable “You are correct, sir.” Their banter became one of television’s most durable partnerships.

Although the sidekick role defined him, McMahon’s career extended far beyond “The Tonight Show.” He hosted the talent competition “Star Search,” which helped introduce audiences to a number of future entertainers, and co-hosted “TV’s Bloopers & Practical Jokes” with Dick Clark. He appeared in films and on other television programs, presided over specials and parades, and became a familiar figure in advertising.

For many viewers, McMahon was also inseparable from the sweepstakes promotions he represented. His image—often associated with the fantasy of arriving at someone’s home with an enormous prize check—became part of American popular culture. He promoted products ranging from beer to financial services, embracing commercial work with the same hearty enthusiasm he brought to late-night television.

Before entering show business, McMahon served as a Marine Corps aviator. He flew training missions during World War II and later flew combat missions in the Korean War, eventually retiring from the Marine Corps Reserve as a colonel. That military background contributed to the discipline and professionalism colleagues said he carried throughout his broadcasting career.

He could command a room with his voice, yet he understood that his greatest contribution often came from helping someone else shine.

McMahon’s achievement was to transform a supporting position into an art. He was not merely an announcer or a man seated beside the star. He became an essential part of the program’s rhythm and identity, and eventually a beloved celebrity in his own right. Later late-night programs would adopt their own announcers, bandleaders and comic partners, but McMahon remained the model against whom television sidekicks were measured.

His legacy rests on a rare kind of generosity in performance. For 30 years, he helped make Johnny Carson look effortless, funny and welcoming. In doing so, Ed McMahon demonstrated that the person beside the star could be indispensable—and could become a star as well.

## Ed McMahon Made Second Billing a Star Turn

For three decades, seven words announced that late-night television’s main event had arrived: “Heeeere’s Johnny!”

The voice belonged to Ed McMahon, Johnny Carson’s longtime announcer, foil and conspicuously cheerful co-conspirator on *The Tonight Show*. From 1962 until Carson’s retirement in 1992, McMahon occupied one of television’s most difficult positions: always visible, rarely central and essential precisely because he never tried to seize the spotlight.

McMahon was widely described as television’s definitive “second banana,” but the phrase understates the range the job required. He introduced Carson, warmed the room, laughed with contagious force and rescued conversations whenever they threatened to stall. He could absorb a joke, feed Carson a setup or turn his own booming confidence into the evening’s punchline. His trademark “Hi-yo!” and expansive laugh became part of the program’s rhythm.

Doc Severinsen, the show’s flamboyant bandleader and another member of Carson’s inner circle, called McMahon “the greatest second banana in the business.” It was a tribute to McMahon’s discipline as much as his personality. The best sidekick had to be quick without looking competitive, prominent without appearing needy.

David Letterman, whose own late-night career was built in Carson’s shadow, remembered the emotional signal carried by McMahon’s voice. “Ed McMahon’s voice at 11:30 was a signal that something fun was about to happen,” Letterman said after McMahon’s death in 2009, adding: “Ed was a consummate broadcaster, a good friend and a gentleman.”

That description—gentleman—recurred in remembrances from entertainers who knew how unforgiving television could be. Joan Rivers called McMahon “one of the last of the true gentlemen in our business.” Rivers, a frequent Carson guest who eventually became his permanent guest host, understood the value of McMahon’s welcome. His enthusiasm could reassure a nervous comic before Carson had even delivered a verdict.

Dick Clark similarly described McMahon as “the epitome of a sidekick” and “an integral part of the success of *The Tonight Show*.” Clark’s assessment pointed to the paradox of McMahon’s career: His performance was designed to appear effortless, yet the program’s ease depended on it. Carson’s cool reserve played better against McMahon’s hearty warmth; Carson’s raised eyebrow became funnier when answered by McMahon’s rolling laugh.

Don Rickles, who made a sport of insulting both Carson and McMahon, exposed another of the sidekick’s strengths. McMahon could take a hit without surrendering authority or good humor. Beneath the televised combat was real affection: Rickles remembered him as “a warm, wonderful man and a great friend.”

McMahon’s career extended far beyond Carson’s desk. He hosted *Star Search*, appeared for years with Dick Clark on *TV’s Bloopers & Practical Jokes* and became the unmistakable face of American Family Publishers’ sweepstakes advertising. He was also a decorated Marine Corps aviator who retired from the reserve as a colonel. Yet every later role drew on the qualities perfected beside Carson: the resonant voice, the genial confidence and the ability to make another person’s big moment feel even bigger.

That was McMahon’s particular genius. He did not merely stand next to the star; he helped create the conditions in which the star could shine. Television has produced countless co-hosts, announcers and on-air partners since then, but few have understood supporting performance so completely.

Ed McMahon turned second billing into an indispensable art—and made “second banana” sound less like a ranking than a title.

Others noted that McMahon’s job required more than introducing the host: he could read Carson’s mood, sustain a joke, rescue a weak moment and draw attention without competing for it.

- **Loyalty:** Friends and fellow broadcasters repeatedly described him as exceptionally loyal—to Carson, to colleagues and to the institutions he supported. His partnership with Carson endured for three decades, and he never tried to turn his prominence into a rivalry with the star.

- **Warmth:** Dick Clark, Jerry Lewis and others recalled a large, genial man whose private warmth matched his public personality. His booming voice and hearty laugh could fill a studio, but colleagues stressed his kindness, generosity and genuine interest in people.

- **Importance to late-night television:** David Letterman, Conan O’Brien and other late-night figures treated McMahon not merely as an announcer but as a foundational part of the format. His entrance call signaled that the evening’s main television event was beginning, while his chemistry with Carson established the model for the host-sidekick relationship followed by later generations.

The tributes shared a central theme: Carson may have been the star, but *The Tonight Show* as audiences knew it would have been difficult to imagine without McMahon’s voice, laughter and steady presence.
